Hello everyone, we are team [team name]. Our project is the Kaggle competition House Prices: Advanced Regression Techniques. Our final score is 0.11624, which put us at rank 257. In the next few minutes we will show how we got there and what we learned.

The task is to predict the sale price of 1,459 houses in Ames, Iowa. We learn from 1,460 houses with known prices, and each house has 79 features, such as living area, quality and neighbourhood. Kaggle scores us with the root mean squared error on the log of the price, so a ten percent error costs the same for a cheap house and for an expensive one.

Our first attempt was a pipeline generated with an AI coding assistant. It scored 0.11745 on Kaggle, which was good, but we could not explain why each part was there. Since this assignment is about the pathway, we rebuilt everything with two rules. Every step changes only one thing, and every step is scored with the same five-fold cross-validation. That way we always knew what each decision was worth.

First, the price is skewed. Its skewness is 1.88, and after a log transform it is 0.12, so we predict the log price. Second, missing values have two meanings: for pool quality, NA means the house has no pool, but for lot frontage it means the value was not recorded. Third, two very large houses sold for less than 300,000 dollars. Both were partial sales of unfinished homes, and they come back later in our story. Now [Member 1] will explain our method.

Thanks. To compare ideas fairly, we use five-fold cross-validation. Each fold of 292 houses is predicted by a model trained on the other 1,168, so every house is predicted once by a model that never saw it. To avoid data leakage, the median filling, scaling and one-hot encoding are refitted inside every fold. Predicting the average price gives an error of 0.408, and a simple Ridge regression gives 0.155.

Then we improved the features one step at a time with the same Ridge model. Predicting the log price and labelling missing values helped a little. Adding total area and house age did nothing, because a linear model can already add columns together. The big jump was step 5: the log of the skewed area features cut the error by twelve percent. Price grows in proportion to size, so on a log scale the relationship is a straight line. This is our answer to the first question.

With the features fixed, we compared seven models. The boosting models, XGBoost and CatBoost, were the best at about 0.123, and Random Forest was the worst, even behind Ridge. The chart shows why. Random Forest averages independent trees, so adding more trees soon stops helping. Boosting adds small trees one after another, and each one fixes the error that is still left, so it reaches a lower error.

Blending only helps when the models make different mistakes. This heatmap shows how similar their errors are. Ridge, Lasso and ElasticNet make almost the same errors, so we kept only Lasso. We blended Lasso, XGBoost, CatBoost and SVR with equal weights, and the CV error dropped to 0.119, better than any single model. We did not tune the weights, because that would only fit the noise.

Then we submitted to Kaggle. Up to submission four, our CV and the leaderboard agreed. After that they did not. Our blend, S6, had our best CV score, but on Kaggle it was worse than our first attempt. Instead of trying more models, we looked at where our errors came from.

We found a blind spot. The two outliers from our data exploration make up seventeen percent of our squared error, and both fall into the same fold, so our CV never learned from one while predicting the other. The test set has a third house of the same kind, house 2550. Because we had removed its look-alikes from training, our models priced it far above the 160 to 185 thousand dollars its look-alikes sold for.

So in step 13 we kept the two houses in training and added one simple feature that flags huge partial sales. Normal cross-validation could not test this, so we built our own check: hold out one outlier, learn from the other, and predict it. The error dropped from about four times too high to under two times. Our prediction for house 2550 fell from 643 to 260 thousand dollars, and the other houses barely changed.

We submitted this change only once. It scored 0.11624, our best score and better than our first attempt. For the second question, our biggest improvement on Kaggle was from S1 to S2, a drop of 0.0114, and our cross-validation shows it came mostly from predicting the log price. But the improvement we learned the most from was this last one.

To sum up, we learned three things. First, change one thing at a time, so you know what each idea is worth. Second, a log transform that fits the shape of the data gave our biggest gain. Third, cross-validation has blind spots, and looking at individual errors helped us more than trying more models. Thank you for watching.
